explanations.explanation: That's what happened. Gilead's wife bore him sons, and when they grew up they drove Jephthah out (Judges 11:2). They told him he would have no inheritance in their father's house. I think that one hurt.

explanations.answer: They make him head of the family
explanations.explanation: Oh, if only. The text goes the other way: the sons grew up and drove Jephthah out (Judges 11:2). Nobody handed him a title or a seat at the head of the table. He got shown the door.

explanations.answer: They give him a share of the land
explanations.explanation: No share for him, friend. The brothers told Jephthah, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house…” (Judges 11:2). That's the opposite of splitting anything with him. They drove him out instead.

Yes, that's the word the brothers used. They said, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman.” (Judges 11:2). His father was Gilead, but his mother wasn't Gilead's wife. That's the line they drew, and it was a cold one.
Close to the idea, but not the word. Jephthah is called a Gileadite right in verse 1, so tribe isn't what the brothers pointed to. They said he was the son of another woman (Judges 11:2).

An inheritance is what the brothers denied him, but land isn't the word they used. They said he would have no inheritance in their father's house because he was “…the son of another woman.” (Judges 11:2). The word is woman. They pointed to his mother.

That's the crowd. Out in the land of Tob, “…worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him.” (Judges 11:3). That's the text's description of them, not mine. Jephthah himself is called a mighty man of valor back in verse 1.
Priests aren't who the text names, friend. It says worthless men gathered around Jephthah and traveled with him (Judges 11:3). Levites aren't mentioned in that verse.

Edomite soldiers aren't who the text names here. Judges 11:3 says worthless men gathered around Jephthah in Tob and traveled with him. Edom shows up later in this passage, when Israel sends messengers to its king and then bypasses its land (Judges 11:17-18).

The elders of Gilead, yes. They went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob (Judges 11:5). Later Jephthah asks them, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house?” (Judges 11:7). I think that made for an awkward knock on the door.
No priests are mentioned here, friend. The text says the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah from Tob (Judges 11:5). Gilead's own leaders made the trip.
Ephraim isn't in this scene. The ones who show up are the elders of Gilead, who went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob (Judges 11:5). The visitors came from Jephthah's own home region.

That's the job offer. The elders said, “Come, be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:6). They were asking him to lead the fight. Verse 1 already calls Jephthah a mighty man of valor.
No priest talk here. The elders asked him to be their commander so they could fight against the Ammonites (Judges 11:6). That's a battlefield job, not a temple job.
Not a servant, friend. They said, “Come, be our commander…” (Judges 11:6). They wanted him out front. By verse 11 the people made him their leader and commander.

explanations.answer: Why come to me now in your distress
explanations.explanation: That's his question. Jephthah asks the elders, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” (Judges 11:7). Honestly, I can't blame the man for asking.

explanations.answer: How much silver will you pay me
explanations.explanation: No money talk in this scene. Jephthah asks why they've come to him now, when they are in distress (Judges 11:7). His question is about how they treated him, not about a paycheck.

explanations.answer: Who will lead my men in Tob
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the text. Jephthah asks, “Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” (Judges 11:7). Nothing in the verse asks who will lead in Tob.

Leader is the word. The elders told him he could “…become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” (Judges 11:8). That's a bigger offer than the first one, which was only to be their commander. They sweetened it, friend.
No scribe job on the table. The elders said Jephthah would “…become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” (Judges 11:8). A scribe holds a pen, and they were offering him the whole region.
Not a prophet. The elders offered him the word leader: “…become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” (Judges 11:8). They weren't asking him to speak for God. They wanted him to lead them.

True. Jephthah asked, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” (Judges 11:9). The man wanted it clear before he said yes. If someone had hurt you once, you'd read the fine print too.

The text says he does ask. Jephthah says, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” (Judges 11:9). So the statement is true. He wanted the deal said out loud before he agreed.

explanations.answer: They call the LORD their witness
explanations.explanation: That's how they sealed it. The elders said, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” (Judges 11:10). They didn't just say it, they put the LORD's name on it. After that, the next step was for Jephthah to go with them.

explanations.answer: They swear by their father Gilead
explanations.explanation: Gilead isn't brought into it, friend. The elders said, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” (Judges 11:10). They called on the LORD, not on a person.

explanations.answer: They write it on a stone
explanations.explanation: No stone, no chisel. Judges 11:10 has the elders speaking: “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” Their promise was spoken, with the LORD named as witness.

Close, but the place is off. The text says Jephthah “…repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah.” (Judges 11:11). He had already left Tob with the elders by then. So this one is False.

False it is. Judges 11:11 says Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, the people made him leader and commander, and he “…repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah.” Tob was behind him by then. Mizpah is the place to remember.

That's the question. Jephthah's messengers say, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” (Judges 11:12). The Ammonites are already at war with Israel, and he asks what's behind it. Straight to the point, and I like it.

Nobody's counting soldiers here, friend. Jephthah's message asks what the king has against him that he has come to fight against his land (Judges 11:12). That's a question about reasons, and no calculator can help with it.
A truce isn't what the message asks about. It asks, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” (Judges 11:12). It's a question about what the king has against him.
That's his demand. The king says, “Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” (Judges 11:13). He says peaceably, but he's already come to fight. That's a polite word on top of an army.
No payment plan here. The king says, “Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” (Judges 11:13). He wanted the land given back.

Moab doesn't get a slice of this one. The king of the Ammonites claims Israel seized his land and tells them to restore it peaceably (Judges 11:13). He wants it handed back to him, with no co-owner in the picture.
Not quite, friend. Jephthah says the opposite: “Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:15). He doesn't give an inch on that. So the statement is False.

False, right. Jephthah's message says, “Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:15). He doesn't admit a thing. Then he starts walking the king through the history to back it up.
Both said no. The king of Edom “…would not listen.” and the king of Moab “…would not consent.” (Judges 11:17). Two doors, two closed. So Israel stayed in Kadesh.
Neither one agreed. Judges 11:17 says the king of Edom would not listen, and the king of Moab would not consent. Two requests, two refusals. So Israel stayed in Kadesh.
Moab turned them down too. The text says the king of Edom “…would not listen.” and the king of Moab “…would not consent.” (Judges 11:17). That's two refusals, not one.

Border is the word. Israel camped on the other side of the Arnon but “…did not enter the territory of Moab, since the Arnon was its border.” (Judges 11:18). Israel stayed on the other side of the line. Jephthah is making a point about the land.
Not a capital, friend. The text says Israel did not enter Moab's territory, “…since the Arnon was its border.” (Judges 11:18). It was the edge of Moab, not the center of it.
No harbor in this verse. Judges 11:18 says Israel did not enter the territory of Moab, “…since the Arnon was its border.” The Arnon marks the edge of Moab's land.
True. Judges 11:20 says, “…Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory.” Sihon was king of the Amorites, and he ruled in Heshbon. Israel had asked politely, and he still said no.
The text says he didn't trust them. Judges 11:20 reads, “…Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory.” Sihon was the Amorite king who ruled in Heshbon. So the statement is True.

explanations.answer: The LORD gives Israel the win
explanations.explanation: That's how it ended. “…the LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, who defeated them.” (Judges 11:21). Sihon had gathered all his people at Jahaz, and it didn't matter. Israel then took possession of all the land of the Amorites who inhabited that country.

explanations.answer: Sihon pushes Israel back to Kadesh
explanations.explanation: It went the other way, friend. The LORD delivered Sihon and all his people into Israel's hand, and Israel defeated them (Judges 11:21). Israel stayed at Kadesh earlier (Judges 11:17), but they weren't pushed back there by Sihon.

explanations.answer: Moab steps in to stop the fight
explanations.explanation: Moab isn't named in this battle. The text says Sihon gathered all his people at Jahaz and fought Israel, and the LORD delivered Sihon and all his people into Israel's hand (Judges 11:20-21). Moab comes up earlier in the passage, when Israel asks its king for passage and bypasses its land (Judges 11:17-18).

explanations.answer: Each side keeps what its god grants
explanations.explanation: That's his point. Jephthah asks, “Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us.” (Judges 11:24). Chemosh is the god Jephthah names as the king's. He sets what Chemosh grants the king beside what the LORD has granted Israel.

Not Chemosh, friend. The one Jephthah calls on to decide is the LORD, the Judge: “May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:27). Chemosh comes up back in verse 24, where Jephthah names him as the king's god. There Jephthah says, “Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us.” (Judges 11:24).

explanations.answer: Both sides should split the land
explanations.explanation: No splitting in the message. Jephthah asks the king whether he possesses whatever Chemosh grants him, and then says, “So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us.” (Judges 11:24). He points to what the LORD has granted Israel.

Three hundred, yes. Jephthah says, “For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon.” (Judges 11:26). That's a long time. Then he asks, “Why did you not take them back during that time?” (Judges 11:26).
Forty isn't the number here. Jephthah says Israel has lived in those cities for three hundred years (Judges 11:26). Forty is a lot, but he's making a much bigger point.

Not eighteen, friend. Judges 11:26 says three hundred years. Jephthah uses that number to ask the king why he did not take the cities back during that time. Three hundred years is a lot of time to bring it up.

Judge is it. Jephthah says, “May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:27). He says he has not sinned against the king, and he asks the LORD to decide. He's laid out his case and leaves it there.

Shepherd is a title for the LORD elsewhere in Scripture, like in Psalm 23:1, but it isn't the one here. Jephthah says, “May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:27). The word he uses fits a courtroom.
No builder in this verse. Jephthah says, “May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:27). It's the word for someone who decides between two sides.
Not this time, friend. Judges 11:28 says, “…the king of the Ammonites paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him.” He ignored the message. So the statement is False.

False is right. The text says the king of the Ammonites “…paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him.” (Judges 11:28). Jephthah gave his full case, and the king brushed it off. This story isn't over.
